title: Winter feeder-bird communities in North America shifted to warmer-adapted species in 2002-2024, but year-to-year and local winter temperature did not explain the shift
abstract: We tested the reported warm shift of winter bird communities at Project FeederWatch sites (Prince and Zuckerberg 2015, eastern North America, 1990-2012). We used 3.49 million public FeederWatch checklists (seasons 2001-2024) and NOAA GHCN_CAMS temperature. The analysis plan was written before the models were fit. The community temperature index (CTI) used species temperature indices from a separate half of the sites and only December-February checklists. With site fixed effects, CTI increased in the East by +0.09 C per decade in 2002-2012 (95% interval -0.02 to +0.19) and by +0.22 C per decade in 2013-2024 (+0.14 to +0.30). The extended early trend predicted the later seasons better than no change (skill +0.65). In the West, an independent region, CTI increased by +0.28 and +0.17 C per decade, but mean winter temperature at the sites did not change. Year-to-year CTI did not follow winter temperature anomalies: -0.006 C per C in the East (-0.022 to +0.010) and -0.037 in the West, against full-tracking slopes of 0.22 and 0.38. Exploratory tests found no lagged response, and 2-degree blocks that warmed more did not gain more CTI. Gains of a few warm-adapted species (for example Carolina Wren, Eastern Bluebird, Anna's Hummingbird, Eurasian Collared-Dove) and losses of irruptive northern finches caused most of the change. Limitations: feeder records mix distribution with feeder use and detection, the series starts in 2001, and we did not test feeder practices, land cover or food crops.

CTI change per 1 C DJF temperature anomaly for the primary analysis and seven pre-specified checks. Circles: site fixed effects and linear trend. Squares: site and season fixed effects. Bars: 95% intervals clustered by season. Dashed line: full-tracking benchmark (spatial slope of CTI on site climate).

Exploratory. Top: species contributions to the pooled CTI change from 2002-2006 to 2020-2024 at fixed sites (grey bars lower CTI). Bottom: within-site reporting-rate trends against species temperature index; point size shows mean reporting rate.

citations.reason: We re-test the reported winter CTI increase after 2012 and in the West (supports the continued increase) and test its temperature explanation (no year-to-year or local tracking).
